prompt.context: Your client, Big Island Surfboards, is a surfboard manufacturer based in Hawaii. The CEO wants to expand the company's product line and revenues and is thinking of entering the market for surfboard wax. It hired you to calculate the market size for wax, and your firm determined that the market size for surfboard wax is about $6 million a year with about 3 million bars sold annually. Your firm also found that the market was fairly competitive with three large global players all based outside of Hawaii controlling about 70% of the market, and smaller niche companies including a few based in Hawaii accounting for the remaining 30%. The client was impressed with our work and believes that its unique brand and connection to Hawaii will enable it to succeed in capturing a piece of the pie. It wants to move forward with entering the market and has now asked us to determine how they should enter the market for surfboard wax.
prompt.question: How would you think about this problem? Specifically, how should Big Island Surfboards enter the market for surfboard wax?

clarifying_info.a: The wax comes in a bar form (similar to soap) and is used to coat the top of the surfboard in order to provide surfers with a surface that their feet can grip.

framework: Market entry options: 1) Build capability organically (manufacture wax internally), 2) Acquire an existing wax manufacturer, 3) Joint venture / partnership, 4) Contract out production and resell under own brand, 5) License the Big Island Surfboards brand to another manufacturer

Profitability analysis for viable options: Price (avg market price = $6M / 3M bars = $2/bar; premium possible via brand), Quantity (market share estimate: 5%-15% = 150k-450k bars), Variable costs (materials: wax/scent; packaging; shipping), Fixed costs (rent, labor, SG&A, marketing)
Evaluate each option on: investment required, speed to market, risk level, control over brand/quality, and revenue potential
Recommended hypothesis-driven approach: eliminate options that don't fit client's risk/control preferences, then quantify returns on remaining options over a 5-year horizon

questions.prompt: Discuss the qualitative pros and cons of each market entry option.
questions.guidance: Option 1 (organic build): significant R&D and manufacturing investment, highest potential return but slowest. Option 2 (acquisition): costly and logistically complex, but provides established product line and distribution. Option 3 (JV): spreads cost and risk, but ties the company to a partner in a potentially complicated venture. Option 4 (contract/resell): enables quick production, but creates dependency on contractor's capacity and willingness. Option 5 (license brand): steady revenue stream but relinquishes control of brand. Strong candidates drive toward a hypothesis, e.g., recommending Option 5 as lowest risk.

questions.prompt: The client has narrowed to two options: acquiring Aloha Surf Wax or contracting out production to Maui Surf Wax. For the acquisition of Aloha Surf Wax, calculate whether the client can earn a return on its investment within 5 years (no discounting required). Aloha sells bars at $2.50 to retailers, COGS is $0.50/bar, annual fixed costs (marketing, SG&A) are $300k/year, it holds 10% of the total market in Hawaii, and the owner's firm asking price is $1 million.
questions.guidance: Candidate should calculate annual revenue, subtract COGS and fixed costs to get annual profit, multiply by 5 years, subtract acquisition price to get net return.

math.setup: Annual revenue = 10% x 3,000,000 bars x $2.50; COGS = 10% x 3,000,000 x $0.50; Fixed costs = $300,000/year; Acquisition cost = $1,000,000

questions.prompt: For the contract production option with Maui Surf Wax: Maui will produce 300k bars/year at a cost of $1.50/bar to the client. The client can sell to retailers at $3.00/bar and expects to sell the entire inventory. Maui charges a one-time setup fee of $100k. Annual fixed costs (marketing, sales, SG&A) are $300k/year. Calculate whether the client can earn a return on its investment within 5 years.
questions.guidance: Candidate should calculate annual revenue, subtract per-unit COGS and fixed costs to get annual profit, multiply by 5 years, then subtract the one-time setup fee.

math.setup: Revenue = 300,000 x $3.00; COGS = 300,000 x $1.50; Fixed costs = $300,000/year; One-time setup fee = $100,000

recommendation: Recommend that Big Island Surfboards enter the surfboard wax market by contracting production out to Maui Surf Wax and reselling the product under the Big Island Surfboards brand.
The contract option yields a $650k net return on an initial $100k investment over 5 years, versus $500k net return on a $1M acquisition investment — better capital efficiency and lower upfront risk.
This approach allows Big Island Surfboards to quickly enter the market and ramp up production without large capital outlay.
risks: Maui Surf Wax may reduce excess capacity devoted to Big Island Surfboards production in the future.
Quality control issues could arise since production is outsourced.
Dependency on a single contractor creates supply chain vulnerability.
next_steps: Conduct due diligence on other potential acquisition targets and contract manufacturers to see if better terms are available.
Explore options the CEO initially ruled out (organic growth, JV) as the business scales.
Negotiate contractual protections with Maui Surf Wax around minimum capacity commitments and quality standards.
